questions.question: Into which three chronological sub-periods is the Neoclassical Period (1660–1785) traditionally divided?
options: The Puritan Interregnum, the Age of Reason, and the Victorian Era
The Restoration Age, the Augustan Age, and the Age of Sensibility
The Elizabethan, Jacobean, and Caroline Ages
The Early Tudor, the Commonwealth, and the Pre-Raphaelite Ages
questions.explanation: The Neoclassical era spans the Restoration 1660-1700, Augustan Age 1700-1745, and Age of Sensibility 1745-1785.

questions.question: Which historical event of May 1660 marks the formal opening of the Neoclassical Period in English literature?
options: The union of the English and Scottish parliaments
The signing of the Treaty of Utrecht
The passage of the Bill of Rights by Parliament
The Restoration of King Charles II to the English throne
questions.explanation: The return of Charles II from continental exile in May 1660 inaugurated the Restoration and Neoclassical era.

questions.question: Which two theatrical patent companies were chartered by King Charles II in 1660 upon the reopening of the London playhouses?
options: The Lord Chamberlain's Men and the Admiral's Men
The Queen's Men and the Prince's Troupe
The Globe Players and the Blackfriars Company
The King's Company and the Duke's Company
questions.explanation: Charles II granted royal monopolies to Thomas Killigrew King Company and William Davenant Duke Company.

questions.question: Which scientific institution, chartered by King Charles II in 1662, promoted plain, clear, and unadorned English prose?
questions.explanation: The Royal Society advocated a close naked natural way of speaking rejecting ornate rhetoric.

questions.question: Which Restoration naval administrator kept a famous secret shorthand diary from 1660 to 1669, recording the Great Plague and Great Fire?
questions.explanation: Samuel Pepys kept his celebrated diary from 1660 to 1669 offering vivid eyewitness accounts of London life.

questions.question: In which year was the first edition of John Milton's blank-verse epic poem 'Paradise Lost' published in ten books?
questions.explanation: Paradise Lost was first published in ten books in 1667 and later redivided into twelve books in 1674.

questions.question: Which 1678 Christian allegory by John Bunyan narrates the spiritual journey of Christian from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City?
options: The Life and Death of Mr. Badman
Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners
questions.explanation: Bunyan published Part I of The Pilgrim Progress in 1678 while Part II concerning Christiana appeared in 1684.

questions.question: Which mock-heroic poem in octosyllabic couplets was published by Samuel Butler beginning in 1663 to ridicule Puritan fanaticism?
questions.explanation: Samuel Butler published Hudibras in three parts in 1663, 1664, and 1678 mocking Presbyterian knights.

questions.question: Who was appointed the very first official Poet Laureate of England by royal letters patent in 1668?
questions.explanation: John Dryden received the formal title of Poet Laureate in 1668 and Historiographer Royal in 1670.

questions.question: Which 1681 biblical allegory in heroic couplets did John Dryden write during the Exclusion Crisis to satirize the Earl of Shaftesbury?
questions.explanation: Absalom and Achitophel uses King David rebellion story to allegorize King Charles II and Monmouth.

questions.question: Which Whig dramatist is crowned the successor to the realm of Nonsense in John Dryden's mock-heroic satire 'Mac Flecknoe' (1682)?
questions.explanation: Dryden lampoons his rival Thomas Shadwell as the dull heir to the Irish poetaster Richard Flecknoe.

questions.question: John Dryden's 1677 blank-verse tragedy 'All for Love; or, The World Well Lost' is a neoclassical adaptation of which Shakespearean play?
questions.explanation: All for Love adapts Antony and Cleopatra to observe the neoclassical unities of time place and action.

questions.question: Which 1668 critical treatise by John Dryden takes the form of a conversation on a barge among four speakers debating dramatic art?
questions.explanation: An Essay of Dramatick Poesie stages a critical debate on the Thames during the 1665 naval battle with the Dutch.

questions.question: Which pioneering female professional writer authored the 1688 prose work 'Oroonoko: or, the Royal Slave'?
questions.explanation: Aphra Behn published Oroonoko in 1688 recounting the tragic fate of an enslaved African prince in Surinam.

questions.question: Who authored the sharp Restoration comedy of manners 'The Country Wife' (1675), featuring the notorious rake Harry Horner?
questions.explanation: William Wycherley wrote The Country Wife in 1675 satirizing London hypocrisy jealousy and marriage.

questions.question: Which 1700 comedy of manners by William Congreve features the celebrated Proviso Scene between the witty lovers Mirabell and Millamant?
questions.explanation: In Act IV of Congreve The Way of the World Mirabell and Millamant negotiate their marriage conditions.

questions.question: Which 1698 polemical pamphlet by the clergyman Jeremy Collier fiercely attacked the profaneness and immorality of the Restoration stage?
options: A Short View of the Immorality and Profaneness of the English Stage
questions.explanation: Jeremy Collier 1698 treatise targeted Congreve Vanbrugh and Dryden accelerating a shift toward moral drama.

questions.question: Which landmark philosophical work published by John Locke in December 1689 described the human mind at birth as a blank slate?
questions.explanation: Locke argued against innate ideas in An Essay Concerning Human Understanding founding British empiricism.

questions.question: Which two writers collaborated on the influential early eighteenth-century periodicals 'The Tatler' (1709) and 'The Spectator' (1711)?
questions.explanation: Steele started The Tatler in 1709 and teamed with Addison to launch the daily paper The Spectator in 1711.

questions.question: What is the name of the amiable Tory country squire from Worcestershire who serves as a central figure in 'The Spectator' Club?
questions.explanation: Sir Roger de Coverley was introduced by Steele and developed by Addison as an affectionate portrait of a squire.

questions.question: In which 1711 didactic poem by Alexander Pope do the famous lines 'To err is human; to forgive, divine' and 'A little learning is a dangerous thing' appear?
questions.explanation: Pope published An Essay on Criticism in 1711 summarizing neoclassical critical rules in heroic couplets.

questions.question: Who is the fashionable heroine whose lock of hair is severed by the Baron in Alexander Pope's mock-epic 'The Rape of the Lock'?
questions.explanation: Belinda modeled on Arabella Fermor has her curl cut off at Hampton Court by the Baron Lord Petre.

questions.question: Which satirical mock-epic by Alexander Pope celebrates the empire of the goddess Dulness and her chosen King of Dunces?
questions.explanation: Pope published The Dunciad in three books in 1728 and expanded it to four books in 1743.

questions.question: Which poetic meter, consisting of rhyming pairs of iambic pentameter lines, served as the signature verse form of Dryden and Pope?
questions.explanation: The closed heroic couplet of rhymed decasyllabic lines was the dominant poetic medium of Neoclassicism.

questions.question: Published in 1726, what is the full original title of Jonathan Swift's four-part satirical masterpiece 'Gulliver's Travels'?
options: A True and Faithful Account of Four Voyages to Unknown Lands
Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World
Memoirs of the Extraordinary Travels of Captain Gulliver
The Life and Strange Surprizing Adventures of Lemuel Gulliver
questions.explanation: Swift published the book anonymously in 1726 as Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World.

questions.question: In Part IV of 'Gulliver's Travels', what name is given to the race of rational horses who govern the repulsive human-like Yahoos?
questions.explanation: In his fourth voyage Gulliver visits the land of the Houyhnhnms horses endowed with pure reason.

questions.question: In his 1729 pamphlet 'A Modest Proposal', what shocking ironic remedy does Jonathan Swift propose to alleviate Irish poverty?
options: Selling poor Irish infants as food for wealthy landlords
Melting down church bells to mint copper coins
Conscripting the entire peasantry into the British Navy
Exporting all Irish woolens duty-free to France
questions.explanation: Swift bitterly satirizes English economic exploitation by proposing that one-year-old children be sold as meat.

questions.question: Which 1704 prose satire by Jonathan Swift uses the tale of three brothers—Peter, Martin, and Jack—to allegorize divisions in Christianity?
questions.explanation: In A Tale of a Tub Peter stands for Catholicism Martin for Anglicanism and Jack for Calvinist Dissent.

questions.question: Which 1728 ballad opera by John Gay satirized Prime Minister Robert Walpole through the characters of Macheath and Peachum?
questions.explanation: John Gay The Beggar Opera was produced by John Rich in 1728 blending Newgate low-life with political satire.

questions.question: In which year did Daniel Defoe publish his realistic narrative 'The Life and Strange Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe'?
questions.explanation: Defoe published Robinson Crusoe in April 1719 launching the rise of realistic English prose fiction.

questions.question: What name does Robinson Crusoe give to the native companion he rescues from cannibals on his uninhabited island?
questions.explanation: Crusoe names his devoted companion Friday to commemorate the day of the week on which he saved his life.

questions.question: Which 1722 novel by Daniel Defoe presents the first-person picaresque confessions of a woman born in Newgate Prison?
questions.explanation: The Fortunes and Misfortunes of the Famous Moll Flanders appeared in 1722 detailing her life of crime and repentance.

questions.question: Published in November 1740, which bestselling epistolary novel by Samuel Richardson bears the subtitle 'Virtue Rewarded'?
questions.explanation: Pamela or Virtue Rewarded tells in letters how the servant girl Pamela Andrews resists and reforms Mr B.

questions.question: Which tragic epistolary novel (1747–1748) by Samuel Richardson depicts a virtuous young woman persecuted by the rake Robert Lovelace?
questions.explanation: Clarissa or the History of a Young Lady is Richardson tragic masterpiece concerning Clarissa Harlowe.

questions.question: Which 1741 burlesque novella did Henry Fielding publish to mock the calculating morality of Samuel Richardson's 'Pamela'?
questions.explanation: Fielding published An Apology for the Life of Mrs Shamela Andrews in April 1741 exposing Pamela as a schemer.

questions.question: In the preface to which 1742 novel featuring Parson Abraham Adams does Henry Fielding define his work as a 'comic epic-poem in prose'?
options: A Journey from This World to the Next
questions.explanation: Fielding wrote Joseph Andrews in imitation of the manner of Cervantes and defined the comic novel in its preface.

questions.question: Who is the benevolent country magistrate who raises the foundling hero in Henry Fielding's 1749 novel 'Tom Jones'?
questions.explanation: Squire Allworthy discovers the infant Tom Jones in his bed and raises him alongside his nephew Blifil.

questions.question: Which Scottish author wrote the vigorous picaresque novels 'The Adventures of Roderick Random' (1748) and 'The Expedition of Humphry Clinker' (1771)?
questions.explanation: Tobias Smollett drew on his service as a naval surgeon for Roderick Random and wrote the epistolary Humphry Clinker.

questions.question: Which eccentric, digressive novel published in nine volumes between 1759 and 1767 was authored by the clergyman Laurence Sterne?
questions.explanation: The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy Gentleman subverts linear narrative with typography and digressions.

questions.question: In which year did Dr. Samuel Johnson publish his landmark two-volume 'A Dictionary of the English Language'?
questions.explanation: Johnson Dictionary was published on 15 April 1755 containing 42773 entries and over 114000 literary quotations.

questions.question: Which 1759 philosophical tale did Samuel Johnson compose in the evenings of a single week to defray his mother's funeral costs?
questions.explanation: The History of Rasselas Prince of Abissinia was published in April 1759 examining the search for happiness.

questions.question: Which critical work (1779–1781) by Samuel Johnson popularized the critical term 'metaphysical poets' in its essay on Abraham Cowley?
options: Lives of the Most Eminent English Poets
A Journey to the Western Islands of Scotland
questions.explanation: Johnson Lives of the Poets comprises fifty-two biographical and critical prefaces including the Life of Cowley.

questions.question: Which Scottish lawyer and diarist befriended Samuel Johnson in 1763 and authored the famous 'Life of Samuel Johnson'?
questions.explanation: James Boswell met Johnson in Thomas Davies bookshop in 1763 and published his great biography in 1791.

questions.question: Which 1751 poem by Thomas Gray opens with the famous twilight line 'The Curfew tolls the knell of parting day'?
options: Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard
Ode on a Distant Prospect of Eton College
questions.explanation: Gray completed the Elegy in 1750 and published it in 1751 honoring the humble villagers buried in the churchyard.

questions.question: Which mid-eighteenth-century poetic grouping, including Edward Young, Robert Blair, and Thomas Gray, meditated on tombs and mortality?
questions.explanation: The Graveyard Poets wrote meditative verse on death and gloom anticipating Gothic literature and Romanticism.

questions.question: Who is the resilient and charitable clergyman narrator of Oliver Goldsmith's 1766 domestic novel 'The Vicar of Wakefield'?
questions.explanation: Dr Charles Primrose endures financial ruin prison and family misfortune with steadfast faith in The Vicar of Wakefield.

questions.question: What is the name of the depopulated rural hamlet mourned in Oliver Goldsmith's 1770 poem 'The Deserted Village'?
questions.explanation: The poem opens Sweet Auburn loveliest village of the plain lamenting rural depopulation caused by enclosure.

questions.question: What is the subtitle of Oliver Goldsmith's 1773 laughing comedy 'She Stoops to Conquer'?
questions.explanation: She Stoops to Conquer or The Mistakes of a Night turns on Marlow mistaking Hardcastle mansion for an inn.

questions.question: Which character in Richard Brinsley Sheridan's 1775 comedy 'The Rivals' is immortalized for her comical blunders in vocabulary?
questions.explanation: Mrs Malaprop Aunt to Lydia Languish gave the English language the word malapropism for verbal confusion.

questions.question: Published in December 1764, which work by Horace Walpole is celebrated as the very first Gothic novel in English?
questions.explanation: Horace Walpole published The Castle of Otranto in 1764 adding the subtitle A Gothic Story in the second edition.
